territory: Benchmark weaknesses in vision/ML: label errors, benchmark saturation, shortcut learning, metric blind spots, train-test contamination; ideas that expose or repair flawed evaluation
title: Label-error sensitivity curves for leaderboard rankings
one_line_idea: Quantify how many adjacent leaderboard rank orderings survive as suspected label errors are progressively corrected, producing a sensitivity curve per benchmark rather than a single cleaned score.
problem: Benchmarks are compared as if labels were ground truth, but nobody reports how sensitive the resulting model ranking is to plausible label-error corrections.
core_hypothesis: Adjacent-rank orderings on mature vision leaderboards are frequently within label-error-induced noise: correcting even a modest, defensible subset of suspect labels flips many nearby pairs while leaving distant pairs intact.
core_claim: Adjacent-rank orderings on mature vision leaderboards are frequently within label-error-induced noise: correcting even a modest, defensible subset of suspect labels flips many nearby pairs while leaving distant pairs intact.
method_sketch: Take public per-item predictions for many models on one benchmark, use a label-error detector plus human verification to build several defensible correction sets, recompute rankings under each, and report pairwise flip rates versus rank distance.
falsifiable_prediction: On at least one mature classification benchmark, correcting a human-verified suspect-label subset flips the ordering of a nontrivial fraction of adjacent leaderboard pairs; if all top-20 orderings survive every defensible correction set, the idea dies.
why_important: If rankings are label-noise-limited, a large share of claimed SOTA distinctions is meaningless, and the community needs sensitivity curves, not point scores.
why_possibly_novel: Label-error detection is well studied, but publishing ranking-sensitivity-to-correction curves as a standard benchmark artifact, rather than a one-off cleaned test set, appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Label-error detection is well studied, but publishing ranking-sensitivity-to-correction curves as a standard benchmark artifact, rather than a one-off cleaned test set, appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take public per-item predictions for many models on one benchmark, use a label-error detector plus human verification to build several defensible correction sets, recompute rankings under each, and report pairwise flip rates versus rank distance.
main_risk: Human verification of suspect labels is expensive and itself disputable, making the correction sets contestable.
kill_risk: Human verification of suspect labels is expensive and itself disputable, making the correction sets contestable.
community_default_belief: Cleaned test sets settle the label-error question: once a benchmark has been relabeled by one effort, rankings computed on it are trustworthy.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A single cleaned version is one draw from a distribution of defensible corrections; ranking stability should be measured across that distribution, and there is no evidence it is stable for closely ranked models.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Use an existing relabeled variant of a popular benchmark as one correction set, bootstrap alternative correction subsets from its flagged items, and count adjacent-pair flips among publicly available model predictions in an afternoon.

title: Disagreement-weighted scoring beats label cleaning
one_line_idea: Score test items weighted by annotator agreement instead of deleting or relabeling disputed items, and test whether the weighted metric predicts transfer performance better than either raw or cleaned scores.
problem: Benchmark repair usually means deleting or flipping disputed labels, which throws away calibrated information about item ambiguity.
core_hypothesis: A soft metric that weights each item by inter-annotator agreement preserves ranking signal from clean items while discounting ambiguous ones, and correlates better with performance on independently collected test sets than raw or hard-cleaned accuracy.
core_claim: A soft metric that weights each item by inter-annotator agreement preserves ranking signal from clean items while discounting ambiguous ones, and correlates better with performance on independently collected test sets than raw or hard-cleaned accuracy.
method_sketch: Collect a few annotations per item on a subset of a benchmark, compute raw, cleaned, and agreement-weighted scores for a pool of public models, and compare each variant's correlation with an external same-task test set.
falsifiable_prediction: Across several models, correlation between disagreement-weighted benchmark score and score on an independent same-task test set exceeds the correlation achieved by raw and cleaned scores; if weighted scoring never wins, the idea dies.
why_important: It offers a cheap, non-destructive repair path for any benchmark that already has (or can sample) multiple annotations, avoiding contentious relabeling campaigns.
why_possibly_novel: Soft labels and annotator disagreement are studied for training, but using agreement weights purely as an evaluation-repair mechanism benchmarked against cleaning is less explored; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Soft labels and annotator disagreement are studied for training, but using agreement weights purely as an evaluation-repair mechanism benchmarked against cleaning is less explored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect a few annotations per item on a subset of a benchmark, compute raw, cleaned, and agreement-weighted scores for a pool of public models, and compare each variant's correlation with an external same-task test set.
main_risk: Agreement weights may mostly track item difficulty rather than label correctness, so the weighted metric could penalize models that are genuinely good on hard items.
kill_risk: Agreement weights may mostly track item difficulty rather than label correctness, so the weighted metric could penalize models that are genuinely good on hard items.
community_default_belief: The right response to label noise in test sets is to clean the labels; evaluation metrics themselves should stay hard and unweighted.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hard cleaning collapses genuinely ambiguous items to one answer chosen by the cleaning protocol, injecting a new arbitrary bias, whereas weighting represents ambiguity honestly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one benchmark subset with existing multi-annotator data, compute the three score variants for ten public models and check which best rank-correlates with an external test set; one day of compute.

title: Anisotropic label errors and class-balanced metrics
one_line_idea: Test whether label errors concentrate in specific class pairs and visual regimes, so that error correction moves class-balanced metrics far more than global accuracy.
problem: Label-error rates are reported as single global percentages, hiding whether errors are uniform or concentrated where they distort per-class conclusions.
core_hypothesis: Label errors are strongly anisotropic, concentrated in a small set of confusable class pairs and acquisition conditions, so per-class and worst-class metrics are far more corrupted than the global average suggests.
core_claim: Label errors are strongly anisotropic, concentrated in a small set of confusable class pairs and acquisition conditions, so per-class and worst-class metrics are far more corrupted than the global average suggests.
method_sketch: Stratify verified label errors from an existing audit by class pair, fit a concentration model, then recompute global and worst-class metrics for public models before and after correction, comparing ranking shifts under each metric.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark with an existing error audit, the distribution of verified errors across class pairs will be much heavier-tailed than a uniform-error model predicts, and correcting them will change worst-class accuracy rankings while global accuracy rankings barely move; if errors look near-uniform, the idea dies.
why_important: Fairness-style and long-tail claims rest on per-class metrics; if those are the most label-noise-corrupted numbers, many per-class conclusions in the literature are unreliable.
why_possibly_novel: Global error-rate audits exist; a systematic anisotropy analysis tied to its differential effect on class-balanced versus global metrics appears less developed; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Global error-rate audits exist; a systematic anisotropy analysis tied to its differential effect on class-balanced versus global metrics appears less developed; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify verified label errors from an existing audit by class pair, fit a concentration model, then recompute global and worst-class metrics for public models before and after correction, comparing ranking shifts under each metric.
main_risk: Existing audits may themselves have sampled errors non-uniformly, confounding measured anisotropy with audit methodology.
kill_risk: Existing audits may themselves have sampled errors non-uniformly, confounding measured anisotropy with audit methodology.
community_default_belief: A benchmark with a low global label-error rate is safe to use for per-class analyses too.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A low global rate is consistent with a few classes being severely corrupted, and per-class metrics divide by small counts exactly where errors concentrate.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Take any published list of verified label errors for a popular benchmark, plot the error count per class pair against a uniform baseline, and recompute worst-class accuracy for a handful of models; a few hours of work.

title: Circularity audit of model-committee label cleaning
one_line_idea: Measure whether cleaning test labels with model committees systematically favors models similar to the committee, by comparing rank shifts for committee-related versus unrelated architectures.
problem: Popular label-cleaning pipelines flag items where strong models disagree with the gold label, but the models doing the flagging belong to the same families being evaluated afterwards.
core_hypothesis: Committee-based cleaning is circular: it preferentially removes items that penalize committee-like models, so cleaned benchmarks inflate scores of models architecturally or data-wise similar to the cleaning committee.
core_claim: Committee-based cleaning is circular: it preferentially removes items that penalize committee-like models, so cleaned benchmarks inflate scores of models architecturally or data-wise similar to the cleaning committee.
method_sketch: Build several cleaning committees from disjoint model families, produce a cleaned test variant per committee, evaluate a common pool of models on each variant, and regress each model's rank shift on its family similarity to the cleaning committee.
falsifiable_prediction: Across cleaning committees built from different model families, the post-cleaning rank improvement of a model will be predicted by its similarity to the committee; if rank shifts are independent of committee composition, the idea dies.
why_important: Cleaned benchmark versions are increasingly treated as the canonical ones, so a systematic pro-committee bias would silently distort the field's reference points.
why_possibly_novel: Concerns about model-assisted relabeling exist informally, but a controlled measurement of committee-similarity bias in cleaned evaluation sets seems rare; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Concerns about model-assisted relabeling exist informally, but a controlled measurement of committee-similarity bias in cleaned evaluation sets seems rare; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build several cleaning committees from disjoint model families, produce a cleaned test variant per committee, evaluate a common pool of models on each variant, and regress each model's rank shift on its family similarity to the cleaning committee.
main_risk: Family similarity is hard to quantify; a crude similarity measure could wash out a real effect.
kill_risk: Family similarity is hard to quantify; a crude similarity measure could wash out a real effect.
community_default_belief: Model-assisted label cleaning is a neutral quality improvement whose benefit is independent of which models were used to find the errors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Items where committee models disagree with gold labels conflate true label errors with items that are hard specifically for that committee's inductive biases, and only the first kind should be removed.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Clean one benchmark subset twice, once with a CNN-only committee and once with a ViT-only committee, and check whether CNNs gain more under the CNN-cleaned variant; one to two days.

title: Crossover items and the growing effective error rate
one_line_idea: Track items where a consensus of successively stronger models contradicts the gold label, and test whether this crossover set grows across model generations, meaning frozen test sets get effectively noisier over time.
problem: A frozen test set's label-error rate is treated as a fixed property, but the errors that matter are the ones that strong models can now resolve correctly and get penalized for.
core_hypothesis: The subset of items where a strong-model consensus disagrees with the gold label and human re-adjudication sides with the models grows monotonically with model generation, so the effective penalty from label errors increases as models improve.
core_claim: The subset of items where a strong-model consensus disagrees with the gold label and human re-adjudication sides with the models grows monotonically with model generation, so the effective penalty from label errors increases as models improve.
method_sketch: For one benchmark, take archived predictions from models spanning several years, define consensus-disagreement sets per generation, human-adjudicate random samples from each, and plot the model-correct fraction over generations.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-adjudicating consensus-disagreement items sampled from model generations of increasing strength will show a rising fraction of model-correct verdicts; if the fraction is flat or falling, the idea dies.
why_important: It reframes benchmark aging quantitatively: saturation may partly be mislabeled headroom, and the effect worsens exactly when leaderboards are most contested.
why_possibly_novel: Individual audits have shown models beating gold labels on some items; a longitudinal, generation-indexed treatment of the crossover set as a benchmark-aging metric appears new; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Individual audits have shown models beating gold labels on some items; a longitudinal, generation-indexed treatment of the crossover set as a benchmark-aging metric appears new; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For one benchmark, take archived predictions from models spanning several years, define consensus-disagreement sets per generation, human-adjudicate random samples from each, and plot the model-correct fraction over generations.
main_risk: Archived predictions for older generations may be unavailable or unrepresentative, forcing retraining that changes the historical models.
kill_risk: Archived predictions for older generations may be unavailable or unrepresentative, forcing retraining that changes the historical models.
community_default_belief: A test set audited once for label errors has a known, fixed noise level that affects all models equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Label noise does not affect models equally: models that surpass the annotator's accuracy on an item class are penalized where weaker models were not, so noise costs grow with capability.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Sample consensus-disagreement items for one old and one recent model cohort on the same benchmark, adjudicate a small random sample of each, and compare model-correct fractions; a day including annotation.

title: Reproducibility floor for segmentation boundary scores
one_line_idea: Estimate the mask re-annotation reproducibility floor of segmentation benchmarks and flag published mIoU gaps that fall below it as unresolvable by that benchmark.
problem: Segmentation papers claim fractional-point mIoU improvements without knowing how much of the metric is reproducible under independent re-annotation of the same images.
core_hypothesis: Independent expert re-annotation of segmentation test sets yields self-disagreement large enough that many published mIoU gaps between competing methods are below the benchmark's reproducibility floor.
core_claim: Independent expert re-annotation of segmentation test sets yields self-disagreement large enough that many published mIoU gaps between competing methods are below the benchmark's reproducibility floor.
method_sketch: Re-annotate a modest random sample of test images under the original annotation guidelines with trained annotators, compute annotator-gold and annotator-annotator mIoU, and derive a floor with confidence intervals; compare to the distribution of claimed gaps in recent papers on that benchmark.
falsifiable_prediction: Re-annotating a random test subset of a popular segmentation benchmark with the original protocol will produce an annotator-vs-gold mIoU noticeably below perfect, and a floor larger than typical claimed method gaps; if re-annotation reproduces gold nearly perfectly, the idea dies.
why_important: It gives reviewers and authors a concrete number below which mIoU claims on that benchmark are unfalsifiable, potentially changing acceptance standards.
why_possibly_novel: Inter-annotator agreement is known to be imperfect, but publishing per-benchmark reproducibility floors as a first-class statistic to gate claims seems uncommon; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Inter-annotator agreement is known to be imperfect, but publishing per-benchmark reproducibility floors as a first-class statistic to gate claims seems uncommon; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate a modest random sample of test images under the original annotation guidelines with trained annotators, compute annotator-gold and annotator-annotator mIoU, and derive a floor with confidence intervals; compare to the distribution of claimed gaps in recent papers on that benchmark.
main_risk: Hiring annotators who match the original pool's training and tools is difficult, so the measured floor may reflect protocol mismatch rather than intrinsic ambiguity.
kill_risk: Hiring annotators who match the original pool's training and tools is difficult, so the measured floor may reflect protocol mismatch rather than intrinsic ambiguity.
community_default_belief: Gold masks are exact, so any mIoU improvement, however small, reflects real model differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Mask boundaries on fuzzy or occluded objects are annotator choices, not facts, so the gold standard has intrinsic variance that bounds resolvable differences.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Re-annotate a small pilot set of test images from one benchmark, compute the annotator-gold mIoU, and compare it against the gaps in a handful of recent leaderboard entries; feasible in days with a small annotation budget.

title: Item response theory as a label-error detector
one_line_idea: Fit item response theory models to the model-response matrix of a benchmark and test whether items with negative discrimination are strongly enriched for label errors and ambiguity.
problem: Label-error detection typically needs training-data access or dedicated detectors, while leaderboards already contain a rich matrix of many models' answers per item that goes unused.
core_hypothesis: Items where stronger models systematically do worse than weaker ones (negative IRT discrimination) are predominantly mislabeled or ill-posed, making the response matrix alone a cheap, model-agnostic error detector.
core_claim: Items where stronger models systematically do worse than weaker ones (negative IRT discrimination) are predominantly mislabeled or ill-posed, making the response matrix alone a cheap, model-agnostic error detector.
method_sketch: Fit a 2-parameter IRT model to public per-item predictions from many models on one benchmark, rank items by discrimination, and human-adjudicate samples from the bottom and middle of the ranking to measure error enrichment.
falsifiable_prediction: Human adjudication of negative-discrimination items will find a much higher label-error rate than in matched positive-discrimination items; if enrichment is weak, the idea dies.
why_important: Benchmark maintainers could audit labels using only submission histories they already have, without new annotation campaigns or training-data access.
why_possibly_novel: IRT has been applied to benchmark analysis, but positioning negative discrimination specifically as a validated label-error detector with adjudicated precision-recall appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: IRT has been applied to benchmark analysis, but positioning negative discrimination specifically as a validated label-error detector with adjudicated precision-recall appears underexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit a 2-parameter IRT model to public per-item predictions from many models on one benchmark, rank items by discrimination, and human-adjudicate samples from the bottom and middle of the ranking to measure error enrichment.
main_risk: Negative discrimination may mostly capture shortcut items that weak models exploit rather than label errors, diluting precision.
kill_risk: Negative discrimination may mostly capture shortcut items that weak models exploit rather than label errors, diluting precision.
community_default_belief: Finding label errors requires either confident-learning style detectors with training access or expensive re-annotation; leaderboard submissions are just scores.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The per-item response pattern across a diverse model population carries strong information about item validity that neither single-model confidence nor aggregate scores expose.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Using an evaluation harness with cached per-item outputs for many models, fit IRT on one benchmark and adjudicate the fifty most negatively discriminating items; roughly a day.

title: Cleaning can hurt external validity
one_line_idea: Test whether cleaned test sets, by removing hard ambiguous items, become easier and less predictive of deployment-like performance than the raw sets they replace.
problem: Cleaned benchmark versions are assumed strictly better, but cleaning pipelines preferentially remove ambiguous, atypical items that resemble real deployment inputs.
core_hypothesis: Cleaning shifts the test distribution toward prototypical easy items, so cleaned-set scores correlate worse with performance on independently collected in-the-wild test data than raw-set scores do.
core_claim: Cleaning shifts the test distribution toward prototypical easy items, so cleaned-set scores correlate worse with performance on independently collected in-the-wild test data than raw-set scores do.
method_sketch: Evaluate a diverse model pool on raw and cleaned versions of one benchmark plus an independently collected same-task wild set, and compare the two rank correlations with appropriate confidence intervals.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of models, rank correlation between cleaned-benchmark score and an independent wild test set will be lower than that of the raw benchmark; if cleaned scores predict wild performance at least as well, the idea dies.
why_important: If true, the field's instinct to adopt cleaned versions as canonical actively reduces the external validity of its main measuring sticks.
why_possibly_novel: Critiques of specific cleaned sets exist, but a direct head-to-head external-validity comparison between raw and cleaned versions of the same benchmark appears rare; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Critiques of specific cleaned sets exist, but a direct head-to-head external-validity comparison between raw and cleaned versions of the same benchmark appears rare; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a diverse model pool on raw and cleaned versions of one benchmark plus an independently collected same-task wild set, and compare the two rank correlations with appropriate confidence intervals.
main_risk: Differences between raw and cleaned correlations may be too small to resolve with available model pools, yielding an inconclusive result.
kill_risk: Differences between raw and cleaned correlations may be too small to resolve with available model pools, yielding an inconclusive result.
community_default_belief: Cleaner labels always make a benchmark better; removing noisy items is a pure win for evaluation quality.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ambiguity in test items is informative signal about real-world input distributions, and deleting it optimizes label purity at the cost of distributional realism.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one benchmark with both raw and cleaned public versions, compute both correlations against any existing wild-collected counterpart using public model checkpoints; an afternoon of evaluation runs.

territory: Benchmark weaknesses in vision/ML: label errors, benchmark saturation, shortcut learning, metric blind spots, train-test contamination; ideas that expose or repair flawed evaluation
title: Annotator-ensemble Bayes floor for saturation calls
one_line_idea: Use multi-annotator disagreement to estimate an irreducible-error proxy per benchmark and compare remaining SOTA headroom against it to decide which benchmarks are actually saturated.
problem: Saturation is declared informally when scores look high, without an estimate of the irreducible error that bounds achievable performance.
core_hypothesis: For several popular benchmarks, an annotator-ensemble-derived irreducible-error proxy shows that remaining headroom is smaller than the typical gap between adjacent leaderboard entries, making further ranking on them uninformative.
core_claim: For several popular benchmarks, an annotator-ensemble-derived irreducible-error proxy shows that remaining headroom is smaller than the typical gap between adjacent leaderboard entries, making further ranking on them uninformative.
method_sketch: Collect several independent annotations on a random test subset of a few benchmarks, estimate irreducible-error proxies with agreement models, and compare current top scores and inter-model gaps against the estimated band.
falsifiable_prediction: On at least one benchmark widely treated as active, the estimated irreducible-error band will contain the current top scores, implying no measurable headroom; if all active benchmarks show headroom well beyond the band, the idea dies.
why_important: It converts saturation from a vibe into a measurable property, telling the community when to retire a benchmark before years of noise-chasing.
why_possibly_novel: Bayes-error estimation is classical, but routine per-benchmark headroom certification from annotator ensembles as a retirement criterion is not standard practice; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Bayes-error estimation is classical, but routine per-benchmark headroom certification from annotator ensembles as a retirement criterion is not standard practice; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect several independent annotations on a random test subset of a few benchmarks, estimate irreducible-error proxies with agreement models, and compare current top scores and inter-model gaps against the estimated band.
main_risk: Annotator ensembles bound human ambiguity, not task ambiguity; models could legitimately exceed the human-derived floor, making the proxy too conservative.
kill_risk: Annotator ensembles bound human ambiguity, not task ambiguity; models could legitimately exceed the human-derived floor, making the proxy too conservative.
community_default_belief: High benchmark scores still leave meaningful room because models remain below 100 percent, so continued ranking is informative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The last few percent may be dominated by items with no single correct answer, where differences between models reflect luck against arbitrary gold choices rather than capability.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one benchmark, annotate a few hundred items with multiple annotators, estimate the disagreement floor, and check whether the top public models already sit inside it; days including annotation.

title: Saturation profiles across metrics, not scores
one_line_idea: Replace single-number saturation judgments with a saturation profile: the same benchmark scored under mean, worst-class, worst-slice, and robustness-perturbed metrics to reveal which axes still have headroom.
problem: Benchmarks are retired or kept based on the headline metric alone, even though headroom may persist under stricter functionals of the same predictions.
core_hypothesis: Benchmarks that look saturated under mean accuracy are typically unsaturated under worst-class and stability metrics computable from existing predictions, so retirement decisions based on the headline number discard usable signal.
core_claim: Benchmarks that look saturated under mean accuracy are typically unsaturated under worst-class and stability metrics computable from existing predictions, so retirement decisions based on the headline number discard usable signal.
method_sketch: For a handful of high-scoring benchmarks, recompute a fixed panel of strict metrics from public per-item predictions of many models and compare inter-model spread and ranking stability across the panel.
falsifiable_prediction: For most nominally saturated benchmarks examined, worst-class or perturbation-consistency metrics will show inter-model spreads several times larger than headline-metric spreads; if stricter metrics are equally compressed, the idea dies.
why_important: It could extend the useful life of established benchmarks for free, avoiding the cost and contamination risk of constant new-benchmark creation.
why_possibly_novel: Individual strict metrics exist, but packaging a standardized multi-metric saturation profile as the criterion for benchmark lifecycle decisions appears unformalized; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Individual strict metrics exist, but packaging a standardized multi-metric saturation profile as the criterion for benchmark lifecycle decisions appears unformalized; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a handful of high-scoring benchmarks, recompute a fixed panel of strict metrics from public per-item predictions of many models and compare inter-model spread and ranking stability across the panel.
main_risk: Strict metrics have higher variance, so larger spreads may partly reflect noise rather than recoverable headroom.
kill_risk: Strict metrics have higher variance, so larger spreads may partly reflect noise rather than recoverable headroom.
community_default_belief: When a benchmark's headline metric plateaus near its ceiling across strong models, the benchmark is exhausted and must be replaced.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The plateau is a property of the averaging functional, not the data; the same items and predictions can still separate models sharply under tail-sensitive metrics.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Take cached predictions for the top models on one saturated benchmark and recompute worst-class accuracy; if spreads stay compressed, the idea fails fast; an afternoon.

territory: Benchmark weaknesses in vision/ML: label errors, benchmark saturation, shortcut learning, metric blind spots, train-test contamination; ideas that expose or repair flawed evaluation
title: Cross-benchmark rank decorrelation as an early saturation alarm
one_line_idea: Test whether a benchmark's ranking agreement with sibling benchmarks starts decaying before its headline metric plateaus, giving an early-warning signal for saturation.
problem: Saturation is detected only after scores visibly plateau, by which point years of low-information comparisons have already been published.
core_hypothesis: As a benchmark approaches saturation, its model rankings decorrelate from same-task sibling benchmarks first, because remaining differences become benchmark-idiosyncratic noise before the mean score flattens.
core_claim: As a benchmark approaches saturation, its model rankings decorrelate from same-task sibling benchmarks first, because remaining differences become benchmark-idiosyncratic noise before the mean score flattens.
method_sketch: Reconstruct time-indexed leaderboards for several benchmark families from public records, compute rolling rank correlations between siblings, and time-align correlation decay onsets against top-score plateau onsets.
falsifiable_prediction: In longitudinal leaderboard data, rank correlation between a benchmark and its siblings will begin a sustained decline before the benchmark's top-score trajectory flattens; if decorrelation only follows plateaus, the idea dies.
why_important: An early alarm would let the community commission replacement benchmarks before, not after, the incumbent stops measuring progress.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-benchmark correlation studies exist as snapshots; using the correlation time-series as a leading indicator of saturation appears untested; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Cross-benchmark correlation studies exist as snapshots; using the correlation time-series as a leading indicator of saturation appears untested; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reconstruct time-indexed leaderboards for several benchmark families from public records, compute rolling rank correlations between siblings, and time-align correlation decay onsets against top-score plateau onsets.
main_risk: Historical leaderboard records are patchy and survivorship-biased, which could manufacture or hide decay patterns.
kill_risk: Historical leaderboard records are patchy and survivorship-biased, which could manufacture or hide decay patterns.
community_default_belief: A benchmark is informative until its scores stop improving; correlation with other benchmarks is a redundancy measure, not a health measure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ranking signal can die while mean scores still creep upward on noise and overfitting, and the death is visible only relationally, against other measurements of the same capability.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one benchmark family with long public history, compute rolling sibling rank correlations and visually compare decay onset with plateau onset; a day of data wrangling.

territory: Benchmark weaknesses in vision/ML: label errors, benchmark saturation, shortcut learning, metric blind spots, train-test contamination; ideas that expose or repair flawed evaluation
title: Residual-error triage of saturated benchmarks
one_line_idea: Classify the remaining errors of top models on saturated benchmarks into label error, ambiguity, and genuine difficulty, testing whether the unsolved remainder is mostly not real headroom.
problem: The last few percent of error on mature benchmarks is implicitly treated as capability headroom worth chasing, without evidence about its composition.
core_hypothesis: On saturated vision benchmarks, the majority of residual errors of top models are label errors or irreducibly ambiguous items, so the apparent headroom cannot be closed by better models.
core_claim: On saturated vision benchmarks, the majority of residual errors of top models are label errors or irreducibly ambiguous items, so the apparent headroom cannot be closed by better models.
method_sketch: Sample residual errors of one or two top public models per benchmark, have multiple adjudicators classify each into a fixed taxonomy, report composition with inter-adjudicator agreement, and compare across benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: Human adjudication of a random sample of residual errors from a top model will attribute most of them to label problems or ambiguity; if a clear majority are adjudicated as genuinely solvable model failures, the idea dies.
why_important: It determines whether continued optimization on mature benchmarks is scientific progress or noise-fitting, informing where the field spends compute.
why_possibly_novel: Error-composition audits exist for isolated benchmarks; a standardized triage protocol applied comparatively across benchmarks with adjudicator agreement reporting seems missing; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Error-composition audits exist for isolated benchmarks; a standardized triage protocol applied comparatively across benchmarks with adjudicator agreement reporting seems missing; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sample residual errors of one or two top public models per benchmark, have multiple adjudicators classify each into a fixed taxonomy, report composition with inter-adjudicator agreement, and compare across benchmarks.
main_risk: Adjudicators may over-call ambiguity on items that stronger future models could still solve, inflating the irreducible share.
kill_risk: Adjudicators may over-call ambiguity on items that stronger future models could still solve, inflating the irreducible share.
community_default_belief: Remaining benchmark errors represent hard examples that future, better models will progressively solve.

title: Goodhart drift rates across benchmark genres
one_line_idea: Estimate how fast optimization pressure decouples benchmark scores from independent capability measurements across benchmark genres, and test whether drift rate is predictable from submission volume and metric gameability.
problem: All benchmarks degrade under optimization pressure, but the field has no comparative measurements of degradation speed or its determinants.
core_hypothesis: The rate at which a benchmark's scores decouple from independent capability measures varies by orders of magnitude across genres, and is predictable from observable features: submission volume, metric gameability, and test-set exposure.
core_claim: The rate at which a benchmark's scores decouple from independent capability measures varies by orders of magnitude across genres, and is predictable from observable features: submission volume, metric gameability, and test-set exposure.
method_sketch: For benchmarks with dated leaderboards and available fresh capability probes, estimate score-versus-capability decoupling over time, extract drift rates, and regress on benchmark features with held-out validation.
falsifiable_prediction: Fitting decoupling curves (benchmark score versus fresh-data capability over model generations) across genres will reveal systematically different drift rates that a feature model predicts out of sample; uniform or unpredictable drift kills the idea.
why_important: Predictable drift rates would let the community schedule benchmark retirement proactively and set expectations for how long any new benchmark stays meaningful.
why_possibly_novel: Goodhart effects are invoked qualitatively; a comparative drift-rate estimation with predictive features across vision benchmark genres appears unattempted; novelty unverified.
novelty_hook: Goodhart effects are invoked qualitatively; a comparative drift-rate estimation with predictive features across vision benchmark genres appears unattempted; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For benchmarks with dated leaderboards and available fresh capability probes, estimate score-versus-capability decoupling over time, extract drift rates, and regress on benchmark features with held-out validation.
main_risk: Independent capability measures are themselves imperfect, and disentangling their drift from the benchmark's is delicate.
kill_risk: Independent capability measures are themselves imperfect, and disentangling their drift from the benchmark's is delicate.
community_default_belief: Goodhart-style decay is an occasional pathology of badly designed benchmarks, not a lawful process with measurable rates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Every proxy under optimization pressure decays; the scientific question is the rate law, and treating decay as anecdote has left the field unable to plan for it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For one old benchmark genre, plot leaderboard gains against replication-set gains across model generations and check for growing divergence; a day with public data.
